title: Bill Russell, camera versus computer
summary: Rose praises Bill Russell as a genuine authority, whose "Parent Style" chapter is a classic, though he thinks Russell blurs form and style. They sort out which jazz record book it appeared in.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Let me mention another name here. Do you think that someone, for instance, like Bill Russell, who's a musician himself, a classical violinist, knows something about the nature of jazz?
Oh, he certainly does. Bill Russell is a genuine jazz authority. And, of course, his, you know...
And I was going to ask you whether he agrees with you on your theory of jazz.
Well, he does, as of the last discussion we had.
Yeah.

Although he does not consider it important, you see. But he's in agreement. Now, Bill's own emphasis is in different areas. And, of course, I would say that if you were going to make a comparison between Russell and me with respect to our general approaches to it, I would say that Russell is a camera and I'm a computer. Probably nobody has the direct relationship, certainly, to the black jazz or the black musicians seen in lives in Russell. He understands and knows more about them and empathizes with them outside of the musical context to a degree that would never be possible for me.
Mm-hmm.

And would also, as a matter of fact, not be particularly within my range of interest. Mm-hmm. And, likewise, Russell doesn't feel a strong responsibility to do any kind of critical work. Not that he has not done it because his chapter in the jazz record book called The Parent Style is one of the great classics of musical analysis.
This is in the jazz record book?
Yes, in David Hall's jazz record book.
Oh, David Hall's. I was thinking of Edward Smith's or Ramsey's, the jazz record book that was put out in 39. That was called the jazz record book.
I'm not talking about Jazzmen.
Right, right, right.
This is a jazz record book. It was edited by David Hall. Now, I believe that Charles Edward Smith and Ramsey both contributed to that.
Oh, okay. I just had the editor mixed up.
Yes. But Russell's article...
Oh, I didn't know he had one in there.
...is one of the greatest and certainly necessarily must command the respect of any kind of a student of the American popular music.
Mm-hmm.

Although I have quibbles with it myself, for example, I have always felt that Russell is not always clear on the differences between form and style. That he would be had he given it sufficient thought.
Mm-hmm.
And, uh, or placed enough importance on it. But, uh, uh, there is no question about, about Russell's theoretical qualifications. They are extremely high.
